questions.question: How do Strategy and Factory separate responsibilities in a pluggable connector framework?
questions.answer: Strategy defines interchangeable behavior behind a common contract, such as extracting records from a specific source. A factory or registry selects and constructs the appropriate implementation from configuration. The caller should not need a growing switch full of connector-specific behavior. I would keep the shared contract narrow, including lifecycle, error and cancellation semantics, while allowing genuine provider capabilities to remain explicit. Adding a new strategy should require registration and implementation, not editing unrelated orchestration. My resume names Strategy and Factory, but the exact interfaces and discovery mechanism need [[HARSH TO FILL: actual types and example extension]]. Naming the patterns is less important than explaining which change becomes localized.

followups.q: Does every connector need identical capabilities?
followups.a: No. Model optional capabilities explicitly rather than force meaningless methods or unsupported behavior into every implementation.

followups.q: What would you test first?
followups.a: Contract tests shared across implementations plus provider-specific behavior and factory selection errors.

questions.trap: Calling a large switch a strategy design while every new connector still changes the orchestrator.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; actual ownership remains bounded by resume facts.

questions.question: How would you add retries and metrics to connectors without mixing them into every provider implementation?
questions.answer: A decorator can wrap the same connector contract and add cross-cutting behavior before or after delegating, while an adapter translates a provider's different API into that contract. I would separate those jobs: adaptation handles data and protocol mismatch, and a wrapper applies a deliberate policy such as metrics or bounded retry. Wrapper ordering matters. Measuring outside retry reports total logical-operation latency, while measuring each inner attempt reports a different useful metric. A circuit breaker can observe attempts or final outcomes depending on placement, so I would decide rather than stack wrappers blindly. Retrying also needs operation idempotency; structural reuse does not make a destructive call safe to repeat.

followups.q: When is inheritance less suitable?
followups.a: When behavior combinations vary independently; wrappers avoid a subclass for every combination and keep provider implementations focused.

followups.q: Can a wrapper conceal cancellation?
followups.a: Yes. It must propagate deadlines, cancellation and failures consistently with the underlying contract.

questions.trap: Applying retry as a generic decoration without considering side effects or the ordering of other policies.

questions.question: How would you model a connector job that can be queued, running, completed, failed or cancelled?
questions.answer: I would define allowed transitions and their preconditions, not just store a string status that any method can overwrite. Starting should require a queued state, and a terminal result should not later be overwritten by a stale progress update. In a multi-worker service, transitions need conditional persistence, such as an expected state or version check, plus an owner or lease model when relevant. Cancellation requested and cancellation completed may need separate meanings because external work may still be running. A state pattern can help when behavior varies substantially by state, but a small explicit transition table may be clearer. Audit events should record the actual transition outcome, not merely the attempted action.

followups.q: Can a Java enum enforce distributed transitions?
followups.a: No. It constrains values but does not atomically coordinate database updates from multiple workers.

followups.q: Why preserve an attempt identifier?
followups.a: A retried or replaced worker can otherwise write stale completion into a newer job attempt.

questions.trap: Treating a status enum as a complete concurrency and lifecycle protocol.

questions.question: A service validates a request, writes three tables, sends an email and formats an API response. How would you split its responsibilities?
questions.answer: I would first identify reasons each behavior changes, then separate orchestration from policies and side effects. An application service can coordinate the use case and transaction, domain code can enforce business rules, persistence adapters can store data, and a notification port can publish the email request. Response mapping belongs at the API boundary. This does not mean one class per verb: the boundary is useful when changes or tests can happen independently. I would also make the database commit and notification handoff failure behavior explicit, since splitting classes alone does not make those effects atomic.

followups.q: Does a class with one public method satisfy SRP?
followups.a: Not necessarily; one method can still contain several independently changing policies.

followups.q: Where does validation belong?
followups.a: Syntax at the boundary, business invariants in the domain operation, and persistence constraints in the database as a final guard.

questions.trap: Interpreting single responsibility as making every small operation its own class.
questions.notes: Unverified design estimate; not a claim about Harsh's implementation.

questions.question: How would you add a new pricing rule without editing a large conditional in the checkout service?
questions.answer: I would identify what varies, define a small rule contract, and let checkout compose the applicable rules from configuration or a registry. Each rule should receive an immutable pricing context and return a decision or adjustment with an explicit reason. Ordering, conflicts, currency rounding and eligibility must remain defined; hiding the old conditional behind a list does not solve those semantics. A new rule should add an implementation and focused tests while existing orchestration remains stable. I would retain a simple conditional if the rule set is tiny and unlikely to vary, because extension points also have maintenance cost.

followups.q: Who decides rule order?
followups.a: An explicit stable priority or composition policy, never incidental map iteration order.

followups.q: When would you avoid a plugin abstraction?
followups.a: When there is one fixed behavior and no credible extension need.

questions.trap: Calling code open-closed merely because a switch moved into a factory while every change still edits central logic.
questions.notes: Unverified design estimate; rule extension is hypothetical.

questions.question: A subclass of a storage interface throws for bulk reads that the base contract appears to support. Is that a safe subtype?
questions.answer: Only if callers can use the subtype without stronger preconditions or surprising failures than the contract promises. I would write the contract in observable terms: supported operations, ordering, null behavior, atomicity and failure modes. If bulk read is genuinely optional, it should be a separate capability or the base contract should state a consistent unsupported-operation result that callers can handle. A subtype must preserve guarantees and may strengthen postconditions, but should not weaken them. Contract tests help expose violations across implementations; inheritance syntax by itself says nothing about behavioral substitutability.

followups.q: May a subtype reject more inputs?
followups.a: That usually strengthens preconditions and can break callers that were valid against the parent contract.

followups.q: What if one implementation lacks bulk support?
followups.a: Expose a separate capability or provide a correct fallback rather than a misleading subtype.

questions.trap: Assuming matching method signatures prove that inheritance preserves behavior.

questions.question: Several implementations of an integration interface cannot meaningfully implement two of its eight methods. What would you change?
questions.answer: I would split the contract around client needs or independently available capabilities, not mechanically create an interface for every method. A basic lifecycle contract might be shared while pagination, bulk transfer or token refresh is represented only where supported. The caller can discover or receive those capabilities explicitly, and unsupported operations should not be disguised as empty success. This keeps implementations honest and prevents consumers from depending on unrelated methods. Before changing the public API, I would inventory actual call sites and define compatibility behavior so existing integrations do not break silently.

followups.q: Is a marker interface enough?
followups.a: Only if it communicates a capability that callers can safely use; otherwise it adds no contract.

followups.q: How can discovery remain typed?
followups.a: Use explicit capability interfaces or a typed capability query with defined absence semantics.

questions.trap: Splitting every method into a separate interface without considering how consumers use them.

questions.question: A domain operation directly constructs a PostgreSQL repository and an HTTP client. How would you invert those dependencies?
questions.answer: The domain or application operation should depend on narrow capabilities it needs, such as loading an account or requesting a quote, while infrastructure supplies implementations at the composition root. This reverses source-level dependencies: business policy no longer imports a database driver or HTTP library. I would keep ports shaped around use cases rather than expose generic CRUD or transport details. Dependency injection can assemble the graph, but it does not itself create a good boundary. Tests can provide deterministic fakes, while adapter tests verify SQL and remote protocol behavior separately.

followups.q: Does dependency injection guarantee inversion?
followups.a: No. It wires objects; the domain can still depend on infrastructure abstractions or leak transport types.

followups.q: Should every class have an interface?
followups.a: No. Introduce a boundary where independent change, substitution or testing justifies one.

questions.trap: Adding interfaces everywhere while application policy still depends on persistence-specific behavior.

questions.question: A change to a tax rule requires edits in the controller, repository and email adapter. How would you reduce that coupling?
questions.answer: I would trace the tax decision from input to side effect and identify which modules own policy versus delivery. The business rule should be expressed once behind a stable use-case or domain boundary, while the controller maps transport data and adapters handle persistence or email. A change then touches the policy and only the integration points whose contracts actually change. I would avoid layering for its own sake: if the tax rule is trivial and fixed, an extra abstraction may add indirection without reducing change coupling. Tests should exercise policy without starting web or database infrastructure.

followups.q: Does package separation guarantee low coupling?
followups.a: No. Imports, shared mutable state and implicit assumptions can still couple separately named packages.

followups.q: What is a useful signal for a boundary?
followups.a: Independent change cadence or a need to substitute and test the behavior independently.

questions.trap: Counting classes or layers instead of checking whether a business change remains localized.

questions.question: Two connector types share authentication but differ in pagination and retry rules. Would you create subclasses from a common base connector?
questions.answer: I would compose the connector from explicit collaborators when authentication, pagination and retry vary independently. A base class with hooks can work when the algorithm is stable and subclasses vary at a few intentional steps, but it becomes brittle when every provider overrides unrelated methods or depends on hidden call ordering. Composition makes each policy replaceable and testable, at the cost of more wiring. I would first define the lifecycle contract, then inject only the capabilities each connector needs. Shared code should be extracted after behavior is understood, not forced into inheritance because two classes currently look similar.

followups.q: When is a base class appropriate?
followups.a: When a stable algorithm genuinely owns the sequence and subclasses vary only defined steps.

followups.q: Can composition become overengineered?
followups.a: Yes. Avoid wrappers and interfaces for policies that do not vary or need independent tests.

questions.trap: Choosing inheritance solely to reuse code, then exposing protected hooks with undocumented sequencing.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: Would you model a customer's postal address as an entity or a value object?
questions.answer: I would decide from domain identity and lifecycle, not from whether the database gives the address a row. If the address has no independent identity and is meaningful only as a customer's current location, an immutable value object is a good fit: equality follows its normalized fields and replacement is explicit. If the business tracks address history or lets users manage an address independently, that history or identity may deserve an entity. Persistence mapping can represent either choice. I would clarify normalization, country-specific fields and retention before fixing the model, because those rules affect equality and update semantics.

followups.q: Can two equal addresses be distinct values?
followups.a: For a value object, equal domain attributes normally mean equivalent values, even if stored in separate rows.

followups.q: Does an ORM surrogate key decide the domain type?
followups.a: No. Storage identity is not necessarily meaningful domain identity.

questions.trap: Calling every persisted object an entity because it has a database primary key.

questions.question: How should a Money value object define equality and arithmetic across currencies?
questions.answer: I would make amount and currency immutable parts of the value, with equality comparing both under a documented scale and normalization policy. Addition is valid only when currencies match; conversion is a separate operation requiring an explicit rate source, timestamp and rounding rule. I would represent decimal amounts without binary floating-point and choose scale rules from the business and currency domain rather than assuming every value has two decimals. Constructors should reject invalid states, and arithmetic should make overflow, rounding and precision behavior explicit. Persistence and JSON formats must preserve the same semantics.

followups.q: Why not store money as double?
followups.a: Binary floating-point cannot exactly represent many decimal fractions, so repeated arithmetic can violate monetary expectations.

followups.q: Should equality ignore scale?
followups.a: Choose and test a normalization rule; 1.0 and 1.00 may be numerically equal but representation policy matters.

questions.trap: Adding different currencies directly or silently converting with an unstated exchange rate.

questions.question: In a domain model, what should an aggregate root control when an order contains many line items?
questions.answer: The order root should own changes that must preserve order-level invariants, such as legal line quantities, currency consistency or whether a submitted order can be edited. Callers request intention-revealing operations through the root instead of mutating its internal collection directly. The root is also the natural consistency boundary for one atomic transaction, not a reason to load an unbounded object graph. If line items have independent scale or lifecycle, I would reconsider the boundary and use explicit coordination. A relational schema may contain several tables, but table count does not define the aggregate.

followups.q: Should every child update load the full aggregate?
followups.a: No. Keep the aggregate bounded; independent operations may require a different boundary or dedicated command.

followups.q: Does one aggregate equal one table?
followups.a: No. It is a domain consistency boundary, not a schema mapping rule.

questions.trap: Exposing child collections for arbitrary mutation and assuming the root still protects invariants.

questions.question: How would you prevent an account withdrawal from making the balance negative under concurrent requests?
questions.answer: The withdrawal operation should enforce the nonnegative-balance invariant at the authoritative write boundary, not perform a separate read followed by an unconditional write. I would use a database transaction with a conditional update such as balance at least the requested amount, checking affected-row count, or use an appropriate lock/version strategy with retry on conflict. The command should be idempotent if callers may retry after timeouts. A domain method can reject invalid amounts early, but the persistence operation must protect against competing transactions. The response should distinguish insufficient funds from a concurrency conflict or transient storage failure.

followups.q: Is an in-memory synchronized method sufficient?
followups.a: Only for one process and one shared object; it cannot coordinate multiple application instances.

followups.q: What if the update affects zero rows?
followups.a: Interpret it through a defined result, such as missing account, insufficient balance or version conflict.

questions.trap: Checking balance in Java and then issuing an unconditional update, leaving a race between the two steps.

questions.question: A customer signup must create a profile and provision an external account. How would you coordinate the two changes?
questions.answer: I would first decide whether both records share one transactional store. If they do, a local transaction may be simplest; a remote provisioning call cannot be made atomic with that database transaction. For the remote case, persist signup intent and an outbox event together, then let a worker provision using a stable operation key and record success or retryable failure. The profile needs a visible pending state, and permanent rejection needs a compensating or support path. The API contract should not promise completed provisioning until that state is confirmed. This trades immediate consistency for recoverable progress across a system boundary.

followups.q: Why not hold a database transaction open during the remote call?
followups.a: It ties locks and resources to network latency while still cannot roll back a remote side effect.

followups.q: Is compensation always a rollback?
followups.a: No. It is a new business action that may itself fail and need tracking.

questions.trap: Claiming one ACID transaction covers a local database and an unrelated remote provider.

questions.question: Would you expose a generic CRUD repository to domain code for an aggregate with strict lifecycle rules?
questions.answer: I would expose operations that reflect the use cases and consistency boundary, such as load-for-submission or save a versioned aggregate, rather than unrestricted create, update and delete. A generic CRUD surface can let callers bypass lifecycle checks or fetch data without the locking and version semantics the operation needs. The repository interface should avoid ORM-specific types so the domain does not inherit lazy-loading behavior. The adapter owns query translation, while transaction boundaries remain explicit in the application operation. I would still avoid making repositories mimic the entire domain model; a query projection can serve read screens separately.

followups.q: Should reads always return domain aggregates?
followups.a: No. Read-only screens often need a purpose-built projection without aggregate behavior.

followups.q: Can the repository own a transaction?
followups.a: It can participate, but orchestration usually defines the business transaction boundary.

questions.trap: Treating CRUD convenience as harmless when it bypasses invariants or concurrency policy.

questions.question: A transfer needs to debit one account and credit another. When is a domain service more suitable than putting the method on either account?
questions.answer: If transfer policy genuinely spans two account entities and belongs to the domain, a domain service can express the rule without making one account an artificial owner of the other. It should remain stateless and operate on domain concepts, while an application service loads participants, establishes the transaction and persists results. I would define how concurrent transfers avoid deadlock, how insufficient funds are handled, and whether both balances share one atomic store. If transfer state must survive across external boundaries, a durable transfer aggregate may be clearer than a transient service call.

followups.q: Should the domain service call an HTTP client?
followups.a: Usually no; keep external orchestration in an application layer or a domain port with explicit semantics.

followups.q: What protects a two-account transfer?
followups.a: A transaction and concurrency strategy covering both updates, with consistent lock ordering where locks are used.

questions.trap: Moving all business logic into a service and leaving entities as mutable data bags.

questions.question: What belongs in an application service for a place-order use case, and what should remain in the domain model?
questions.answer: The application service coordinates the use case: authorize the caller, load required aggregates, invoke domain operations, persist changes and arrange external work. The domain model decides business meaning, such as whether the order can be submitted and whether its lines are valid. Transport parsing and response formatting stay at the API boundary. I would keep orchestration readable and avoid duplicating domain rules in controllers. The service's transaction should cover local state changes, not a long-running provider call. A focused unit test can verify orchestration decisions, while domain tests cover invariants and adapter tests cover persistence.

followups.q: Can an application service contain conditionals?
followups.a: Yes, orchestration decisions belong there; domain policy should not be copied there as ad hoc rules.

followups.q: Should it return an entity directly to REST?
followups.a: Usually map to an explicit response so persistence and domain internals do not leak.

questions.trap: Equating a thin application service with one that contains no decisions or transaction ownership.

questions.question: How would you publish an OrderPlaced event without losing it if the process stops after the database commit?
questions.answer: I would write the order change and an outbox row in the same database transaction. A separate publisher claims unsent rows, publishes them, then marks delivery, using leases or safe concurrency so several workers do not corrupt progress. A crash after publishing but before marking can produce a duplicate, so consumers must deduplicate by stable event ID or make the effect idempotent. The outbox gives atomic recording of intent, not exactly-once delivery. I would monitor oldest pending age and retry counts, and define a poison-event path that preserves the record for investigation.

followups.q: Can marking sent happen before publishing?
followups.a: That risks permanent loss if the process stops after the mark but before the broker accepts the event.

followups.q: Does the outbox eliminate duplicates?
followups.a: No. It makes intent durable; delivery and consumer effects still need retry-safe semantics.

questions.trap: Calling an outbox exactly-once delivery or marking rows sent before broker acknowledgment.

questions.question: When would a domain factory be useful for constructing a valid, multi-step aggregate?
questions.answer: A domain factory is useful when creation requires a meaningful set of coordinated inputs or must establish several invariants that would make a public constructor unwieldy. It should return a valid aggregate or a clear domain failure, rather than expose a partially initialized object. The factory can select a concrete implementation when that choice is domain policy, but infrastructure wiring belongs in the composition root. I would keep ordinary value construction simple and avoid a factory class that merely renames a constructor. Tests should prove the created object starts in valid states and that invalid combinations are rejected.

followups.q: Should a factory query a database?
followups.a: Usually keep lookup and orchestration outside; use a factory for construction from already-resolved domain inputs.

followups.q: Is every static create method a Factory pattern?
followups.a: No. The value is in hiding meaningful construction complexity or policy, not the method name.

questions.trap: Introducing an abstract factory for a simple object or allowing it to return an invalid partially built aggregate.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: How would you represent a reusable eligibility rule that combines age, account status and region?
questions.answer: I would model each eligibility condition as a named predicate over a stable candidate context, then compose them with explicit all-of, any-of or negate operations. This makes rule combinations readable and testable without burying policy in a long conditional. If rules are persisted or authored by operations, I would define a constrained rule language rather than deserialize arbitrary executable code. Evaluation should return reasons as well as a boolean when callers need explainability. I would version policy changes and decide which version applies to an in-flight decision, since repeat evaluation later may otherwise yield a different outcome.

followups.q: Would you compile user-entered Java expressions?
followups.a: No. Use a constrained, validated representation with explicit supported operators and limits.

followups.q: Why return a reason?
followups.a: It supports useful diagnostics and audit without asking callers to reconstruct policy decisions.

questions.trap: Building an unrestricted expression engine when a small, typed set of predicates is enough.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: A document workflow has different legal actions in Draft, Submitted, Approved and Rejected states. When is a State pattern useful?
questions.answer: I would use state-specific behavior when each state has enough distinct rules that a transition table or guarded methods becomes difficult to read. The current state can own allowed operations and produce the next state, while the aggregate still protects shared invariants and persists the transition atomically. For a handful of simple transitions, an enum plus explicit transition function is often clearer and easier to serialize. If state objects are used, they should not become an uncontrolled second source of truth beside a persisted status. Tests should cover every allowed edge and representative forbidden edge.

followups.q: Does State pattern replace a persisted status?
followups.a: Not necessarily; persisted state remains a durable fact, while behavior objects can be an implementation detail.

followups.q: How do you prevent illegal transitions?
followups.a: Make transition operations explicit and enforce expected-current-state checks at the persistence boundary.

questions.trap: Creating one state class per enum value when behavior is just a small transition table.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: How would you distinguish a rejected business command from a temporary infrastructure failure?
questions.answer: I would model expected business outcomes explicitly, such as insufficient inventory or an invalid state transition, and keep them separate from unexpected database or network failures. The application boundary can map known domain outcomes to stable API responses, while infrastructure exceptions retain retry and alerting semantics. A result type is useful when callers must handle a closed set of outcomes; exceptions can still represent exceptional failures. I would not catch every exception and convert it into a generic rejection, because that hides outages and may tell a client not to retry when recovery is appropriate. Logs should carry a correlation identifier without exposing secrets.

followups.q: Should every validation error be an exception?
followups.a: No. Expected rejected input can be a normal typed outcome if that makes control flow clearer.

followups.q: What should a client receive for an unknown database outage?
followups.a: A generic safe server error, while internal telemetry preserves the actionable cause.

questions.trap: Converting all failures into a successful response with an error message or one indistinguishable status.

questions.question: Where would you enforce a maximum of one active subscription per customer?
questions.answer: I would express the rule in the domain operation so callers receive a meaningful rejection, and enforce it in the database so concurrent requests cannot both pass a prior read. Depending on the schema, a unique constraint or partial unique index can provide the final atomic guard. The application translates that specific constraint violation into a conflict outcome, while unrelated persistence failures remain failures. I would clarify how cancelled, expired or soft-deleted subscriptions count and make the index predicate match that definition. Tests should include two concurrent attempts, not just sequential service calls.

followups.q: Can an application-level existence check enforce uniqueness?
followups.a: No. Two transactions can both observe absence before either commits.

followups.q: What should the API return on a competing create?
followups.a: A documented conflict or existing-resource result consistent with the idempotency contract.

questions.trap: Relying on check-then-insert logic without an authoritative uniqueness constraint.

questions.question: How would you stop a stale administrator edit from overwriting a newer update to the same record?
questions.answer: I would attach a version or equivalent change token to the record, return it when the client reads, and require it on update. The persistence write compares the expected version and advances it atomically; if another writer changed the record first, the update affects no row or raises a conflict. The API should expose a stable conflict response and let the user reload or merge, rather than silently retry the stale values. Optimistic concurrency works well when conflicts are relatively uncommon; frequent contention may need serialization or finer-grained records. The version protects lost updates, not arbitrary business invariants across several records.

followups.q: Should the server transparently retry with the new version?
followups.a: Not for an edit based on stale user intent; that would reapply old values over newer work.

followups.q: Does one version protect two aggregates?
followups.a: No. Cross-record invariants need a transaction or a coordination strategy spanning those records.

questions.trap: Incrementing a version without requiring the caller's expected version during the write.

questions.question: A username must be unique, but two signup requests can arrive at the same time. What is the safe design?
questions.answer: Normalize the username according to a documented case and Unicode policy, then enforce uniqueness on that canonical value with a database constraint. An application lookup can provide a friendly early response, but the insert is authoritative because simultaneous requests can both pass the lookup. The losing request maps the known unique violation to a conflict and must not leak raw SQL details. If signup also sends verification email, persist an idempotent intent so a retry does not create duplicate accounts or messages. I would test concurrent requests against the real database engine used in production.

followups.q: Should the unique key use the display name?
followups.a: Usually store a canonical comparison key separately so presentation does not define identity accidentally.

followups.q: Is an in-memory lock enough?
followups.a: No for multiple application instances or restarts; the shared authoritative store must enforce uniqueness.

questions.trap: Treating a pre-insert existence query as a concurrency guarantee.

questions.question: How would you make a create-order command safe when the caller retries after a timeout?
questions.answer: The caller supplies a key scoped to its identity and operation, and the service stores that key with a fingerprint of the meaningful request and the resulting resource or response. In one transaction, a new key reserves the operation and creates the order; a repeated matching key returns the recorded outcome. Reusing the key with a different payload is a conflict, not permission to mutate the first order. Retention must exceed the retry window and account for privacy or storage limits. This handles duplicate requests at this boundary, but downstream effects still need their own idempotency or durable handoff.

followups.q: What if the first request is still processing?
followups.a: Return a defined in-progress response or wait within a bounded policy; do not launch a second operation.

followups.q: Does this guarantee every downstream action runs once?
followups.a: No. Each side-effect boundary requires its own deduplication or retry-safe contract.

questions.trap: Using an unscoped key or accepting the same key for a materially different request.

questions.question: How would you ensure a repository lookup cannot return another tenant's invoice when IDs are globally unique?
questions.answer: Tenant identity should come from authenticated, trusted request context, not from a caller-controlled body field alone. The application passes that scope explicitly into repository operations, and queries include tenant ID even when the invoice ID is globally unique. Where supported, database row-level controls or composite foreign keys provide another guard, but they do not replace authorization. I would make cross-tenant reads indistinguishable from missing records when that protects existence, and audit denied access. Tests should deliberately create identical local identifiers across tenants and verify every query path, including background jobs.

followups.q: Can a globally unique ID replace tenant authorization?
followups.a: No. Unpredictability or uniqueness is not an access-control check.

followups.q: Where does a scheduled worker get tenant scope?
followups.a: From durable job metadata that is validated and propagated explicitly, not ambient thread state.

questions.trap: Trusting a tenant ID supplied by the client or relying on hard-to-guess identifiers.

questions.question: How would you divide request validation, domain validation and database constraints for a product quantity?
questions.answer: At the API boundary I would reject malformed representation, such as a missing or nonnumeric quantity, with a clear client error. The domain constructor or operation would enforce business meaning, such as quantity being positive and within a product-specific limit. The database would enforce durable structural constraints and protect writes from races or alternate code paths. These checks overlap intentionally but should have one authoritative definition and consistent messages where practical. I would not place cross-record business policy in a database check that cannot express it safely. Tests should cover each boundary and verify that invalid input never creates partial state.

followups.q: Should validation happen only at the API?
followups.a: No. Other entry points and concurrent writes can bypass it; domain and storage boundaries still need protection.

followups.q: Should the database duplicate every business rule?
followups.a: No. Use constraints for durable invariants the database can reliably enforce.

questions.trap: Treating bean validation on one REST endpoint as protection for every path into the domain.

questions.question: A dashboard needs a joined view of orders and delivery status. Must it load and mutate the full domain aggregate?
questions.answer: No. A read path can use a projection tailored to the dashboard, joining or precomputing the fields it needs without exposing mutation methods. The command path should still load the consistency boundary required to enforce business rules. Separating those models avoids forcing a rich aggregate to serve every reporting query and can reduce data transfer. I would begin with a direct query and introduce a separately maintained read model only when measured scale or latency justifies its consistency cost. If the projection is asynchronous, the UI and API must tolerate and communicate its freshness semantics.

followups.q: Does a separate read model imply eventual consistency?
followups.a: Often, but not necessarily; the consistency guarantee depends on how it is updated and read.

followups.q: Should every screen get its own schema?
followups.a: No. Split only when query needs or scale make the simpler model inadequate.

questions.trap: Introducing full CQRS infrastructure before identifying an actual read-model bottleneck or consistency requirement.

questions.question: How would you make an expiry rule deterministic in tests and correct across time zones?
questions.answer: I would inject a clock or pass an explicit instant into the policy, then compare instants rather than relying on the machine's default zone or current time. The domain should define whether expiry is inclusive at the boundary and whether a business date uses a named region such as Asia/Kolkata. Persistence should store an unambiguous instant and preserve any zone needed to explain a local schedule. Tests can freeze time immediately before, at and after the boundary. This prevents flaky tests and avoids hidden dependence on when or where a server runs.

followups.q: Is UTC enough for every schedule?
followups.a: Store instants consistently, but retain a named zone when rules depend on local civil time and daylight changes.

followups.q: Why not mock a static current-time call?
followups.a: A clock dependency is explicit, composable and easier to use consistently across policy code.

questions.trap: Using server-local time and assuming every calendar day is exactly 24 hours.

questions.question: Several payment methods advertise the same general interface. How should a request select one deterministically?
questions.answer: I would register each implementation under a stable explicit key and resolve that key from validated request or configuration data. Registration should reject duplicate keys at startup instead of silently letting classpath order choose a winner. If selection uses capabilities or priority, define tie-breaking and expose the chosen implementation in diagnostics without logging sensitive request data. The registry should return a typed not-found or unsupported result, not null. This isolates additions from orchestration while keeping selection predictable and testable. For a small fixed set, a simple injected map is often enough; a dynamic plugin loader adds operational complexity.

followups.q: Should map iteration choose the default?
followups.a: No. Selection order must be explicit and stable across runtime versions and deployments.

followups.q: When is dynamic loading justified?
followups.a: When independent deployment or runtime discovery is a real requirement with a security and compatibility model.

questions.trap: Resolving providers by simple class name or whichever bean happens to be encountered first.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: A plugin owns an HTTP connection pool and background scheduler. How should the host manage its lifecycle?
questions.answer: The plugin contract should make initialization, readiness and shutdown explicit, with resource ownership assigned to one component. The host starts plugins in a defined order, reports readiness only after required resources are available, and closes them with a bounded deadline during shutdown. A failed initializer must clean up resources it already acquired. Requests should stop entering a plugin before its pool is closed, and shutdown should not block forever on an unresponsive worker. I would avoid hidden static pools because they evade lifecycle management. Tests should verify both normal closure and partial-startup failure cleanup.

followups.q: Should close throw on every cleanup issue?
followups.a: Collect and report cleanup failures while continuing to release independent resources.

followups.q: What if shutdown exceeds its deadline?
followups.a: Stop waiting, record the failure and rely on process termination policy rather than hang indefinitely.

questions.trap: Providing plugin initialization but no defined cleanup or failed-start rollback behavior.

questions.question: How would you evolve a connector SPI without breaking separately maintained implementations?
questions.answer: I would define compatibility expectations first: source compatibility, binary compatibility, runtime behavior and supported implementation versions are different promises. Prefer additive capability interfaces or versioned contracts over adding abstract methods that every existing provider must implement. If a default method is considered, verify its semantics are safe for every implementation rather than merely convenient. The host can validate plugin version and required capabilities at startup, with a clear rejection message. Contract tests should run against representative old and current providers. A deprecation period and migration guide reduce surprise, but do not replace automated compatibility checks.

followups.q: Does a Java default method always preserve behavior?
followups.a: No. It may compile but provide incorrect semantics for a provider with different capabilities.

followups.q: How should an unsupported version fail?
followups.a: Fail fast during startup with the expected range and detected plugin version.

questions.trap: Assuming additive source changes are harmless to already compiled external plugins.

questions.question: A connector may support pagination, bulk writes or incremental sync. How should callers learn what it can do?
questions.answer: I would represent capabilities explicitly as typed contracts or immutable metadata returned during initialization, and validate the requested operation before work begins. A capability should include relevant limits or semantics, not just a boolean: bulk write may have a maximum batch size, and incremental sync needs a cursor contract. Callers should choose a supported path or return a clear unsupported-operation result. Capability data should be stable for the lifetime of a job or versioned if it can change. This avoids probing by executing a potentially destructive method and catching an unsupported exception.

followups.q: Can a boolean supportsBulk be enough?
followups.a: Only for a true binary capability; callers often also need batch size, ordering and partial-failure guarantees.

followups.q: Should support be inferred from exceptions?
followups.a: No. Discover it before invocation so failures are not confused with actual provider errors.

questions.trap: Using one broad interface that promises optional operations and discovering support after a side effect starts.

questions.question: How should a plugin system handle a configuration that names an unknown implementation or omits a required field?
questions.answer: I would parse configuration into a typed object, validate required fields and cross-field rules, then resolve the implementation before reporting the application ready. Errors should identify the configuration path and expected values without echoing credentials. Secret references should be resolved through a secret provider and excluded from logs. For reloadable configuration, build and validate a replacement snapshot completely before atomically publishing it, so readers never observe a half-updated state. Invalid configuration should fail fast at startup or reject the reload while the last-known-good snapshot remains active, depending on operational policy.

followups.q: Should the service silently ignore an unknown plugin key?
followups.a: No. Silent fallback can route work to the wrong implementation and conceal deployment mistakes.

followups.q: How do you avoid leaking secrets in validation errors?
followups.a: Report field paths and constraint names, but redact values and secret-provider responses.

questions.trap: Starting with defaults after invalid configuration without making the fallback visible or intentional.

questions.question: Several validation rules can reject an import row. How do you make the reported errors stable and useful?
questions.answer: I would give each rule a stable identifier and define whether validation is fail-fast or accumulates independent errors. If errors are accumulated, sort them by a documented field and rule order instead of relying on hash-map iteration. Each result should identify the row or field, a safe message, and whether correction is possible; it should not include secret input. Rules that depend on earlier normalized values should run after parsing and normalization, while independent checks can be composed. Deterministic output makes tests, support workflows and repeated imports much easier to reason about.

followups.q: Should validation stop at the first error?
followups.a: Choose based on cost and user workflow; independent cheap errors can often be reported together.

followups.q: How do you preserve deterministic order?
followups.a: Use an explicit ordered rule collection and stable output sort keys, not incidental collection order.

questions.trap: Returning whichever error happens to arise first from nondeterministic parallel validation.

questions.question: When is a Builder a good fit for constructing an immutable request with many optional settings?
questions.answer: A builder helps when a value has several optional or named inputs and callers would otherwise face a long positional constructor or many ambiguous overloads. The builder collects choices, validates required combinations at build time, and returns an immutable value with defensive copies where needed. It should not permit inconsistent intermediate states to escape. For a small object with two required fields, a constructor or factory is simpler. I would also decide whether repeated build calls are supported and whether the builder itself is thread-confined; the immutable result, rather than the builder, is the object to share safely.

followups.q: Should setters remain on the built object?
followups.a: No, not if the goal is an immutable request value.

followups.q: Can build be called twice?
followups.a: Define it explicitly; usually each call should produce a valid snapshot independent of later builder changes.

questions.trap: Adding a Builder to every class even when a concise constructor expresses the invariants clearly.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: A shared token cache is currently a static singleton. What risks would you inspect before keeping that design?
questions.answer: I would check lifecycle, thread safety, test isolation, configuration ownership and whether the required scope is one instance per process, application context or tenant. A static singleton can hide global mutable state and make replacement or cleanup difficult; it also does not create one instance across multiple service replicas. If one process-wide cache is genuinely needed, an explicitly managed singleton bean with clear thread-safety and shutdown semantics is usually easier to test. Sensitive token values need expiry and secure handling regardless of construction pattern. I would not confuse singleton scope with distributed cache consistency.

followups.q: Does singleton guarantee thread safety?
followups.a: No. Instance count and concurrent access safety are separate concerns.

followups.q: Does one singleton span Kubernetes replicas?
followups.a: No. Each process has its own instance unless state is moved to a shared service.

questions.trap: Claiming a singleton is globally unique or inherently thread-safe.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: How would you notify independent modules when an order changes, without making the order call every consumer directly?
questions.answer: For in-process observers, publish a typed event after the domain operation and let registered listeners react, while defining ordering, exception isolation and lifecycle. If listeners perform durable external effects, an in-memory callback is insufficient because a process crash can lose delivery; persist an outbox event with the state change and publish asynchronously. Consumers must tolerate duplicates and should not block the request indefinitely. The event should describe a meaningful fact rather than expose mutable aggregate internals. I would choose an in-process mechanism for local decoupling and a broker-backed mechanism only when durability or cross-process delivery requires it.

followups.q: Should an observer mutate the publisher's aggregate?
followups.a: Avoid it; that makes behavior order-dependent and undermines ownership of invariants.

followups.q: Does an in-memory event bus guarantee delivery?
followups.a: No. Process termination can lose events unless durable intent is recorded.

questions.trap: Treating an in-memory observer callback as reliable integration messaging.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: How would you compose authentication checks that may reject a request before it reaches business logic?
questions.answer: A chain can represent ordered checks such as credential parsing, token validation, tenant authorization and request policy, with each step either rejecting or passing a typed context to the next. I would make the order explicit because authorization before trustworthy identity resolution is unsafe, and define whether a check may short-circuit or enrich context. Cross-cutting framework filters may already provide this pipeline, so a custom chain is justified only for domain-specific composition. Each handler should have clear failure mapping and must not log bearer tokens. Tests should cover order, rejection and context propagation.

followups.q: Can checks run in parallel?
followups.a: Only when independent and when doing so preserves failure semantics; security checks often have ordering dependencies.

followups.q: Should each handler map errors to HTTP?
followups.a: Keep transport mapping at the API boundary so the chain can remain transport-independent.

questions.trap: Reordering authorization ahead of authentication or building a custom chain that duplicates the framework pipeline.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: A batch import has a fixed parse-validate-save sequence but provider-specific parsing. Would Template Method fit?
questions.answer: Template Method can fit if the sequence is genuinely invariant and only a small, stable step varies. A base workflow can make ordering explicit, while subclasses supply parsing or mapping behavior. I would define failure, resource cleanup and transaction semantics in the template so implementations cannot accidentally skip mandatory steps. If providers vary across several independent dimensions, composition through injected parser, validator and writer collaborators is easier to combine and test. I would compare both with actual variation points before choosing. The pattern is not valuable merely because every importer can be forced into the same inheritance tree.

followups.q: What should be final in the base workflow?
followups.a: Mandatory sequencing and invariant-preserving steps that subclasses must not reorder.

followups.q: What if parsing and storage both vary independently?
followups.a: Prefer composition so combinations do not require subclasses for every pair of choices.

questions.trap: Using inheritance when multiple independent variation axes create a subclass explosion.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: A third-party SDK uses callbacks and provider-specific result objects. How would you adapt it to a synchronous domain port?
questions.answer: I would place an adapter at the infrastructure boundary that translates domain requests to SDK calls, maps provider responses into stable domain results, and converts known provider errors into explicit categories. The domain port should not expose SDK classes or callback conventions. If the SDK is asynchronous, the adapter must define timeout, cancellation and thread-pool behavior rather than block an unbounded thread. I would preserve diagnostic provider codes in structured internal telemetry while redacting credentials and sensitive payloads. Contract tests can verify translation, and a small fake SDK can exercise callback races and failure mapping.

followups.q: Should the domain port return the SDK response?
followups.a: No. That couples business policy to a replaceable provider library.

followups.q: What if the SDK callback never fires?
followups.a: Apply a bounded timeout and propagate cancellation with a defined failure outcome.

questions.trap: Renaming provider types without translating their semantics or exposing them throughout the domain.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: Several SDK clients, token refresh calls and request headers are needed to fetch one report. How could a Facade help?
questions.answer: A facade can offer one cohesive report-fetch operation while coordinating token acquisition, provider calls and response assembly behind a smaller contract. It should hide incidental subsystem sequencing, not conceal important business choices such as authorization, retry safety or partial-result behavior. I would keep configuration and resource ownership explicit, inject underlying clients for testing, and return a domain-level result. If callers need different workflow combinations, a single facade may become a god object; split by use case or expose narrower ports. Tests should assert observable behavior without depending on the internal call sequence unless that order is contractually required.

followups.q: Is a facade always a singleton?
followups.a: No. Construction scope is separate from the pattern's simplifying interface.

followups.q: How do you avoid a god facade?
followups.a: Keep it aligned to a use case and split unrelated workflows into separate collaborators.

questions.trap: Hiding retries or authorization policy behind a convenience method with unclear failure semantics.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: How could a proxy enforce tenant authorization before exposing a sensitive document service?
questions.answer: A proxy can implement the same service contract while checking trusted caller identity and document access before delegating. It can also centralize caching or remote access, but those concerns should not blur authorization rules. The underlying service should not be reachable through an unguarded path that bypasses the proxy; dependency wiring and module visibility matter. Authorization decisions need a clear policy source and should fail closed when it is unavailable if the data is sensitive. I would audit the decision safely and test both allowed and denied cases, including tenant mismatch and expired identity context.

followups.q: Does the proxy alone guarantee security?
followups.a: Only if every access path is forced through it and the policy is correct; defense in depth still matters.

followups.q: Can the same proxy cache results?
followups.a: Yes, but cache keys and invalidation must include authorization scope and policy changes.

questions.trap: Assuming a proxy protects data when callers can inject or access the target directly.
questions.notes: Unverified design-pattern question; GAP status follows mock-interview readiness.

questions.question: Design a small notification dispatcher that respects a user's channel preferences and quiet hours.
questions.answer: I would separate the notification intent from channel delivery. A preference policy decides whether email, SMS or push is allowed at the event time, including the user's zone and quiet-hour rule; a dispatcher then selects a configured channel adapter. Persist a delivery attempt with a stable notification ID so retries do not create duplicate logical messages. A quiet-hours decision may schedule a later send rather than discard it, which needs an explicit expiry rule. Provider failures should be classified as retryable or permanent, and channel-specific payloads should not leak into the preference model.

followups.q: What if preferences change after queuing?
followups.a: Define whether policy is evaluated at enqueue or send time; sensitive consent is often checked immediately before delivery.

followups.q: Can retries ignore quiet hours?
followups.a: No, delivery attempts should honor the same policy and expiry semantics.

questions.trap: Treating preference as a one-time routing choice and ignoring changes or local time rules.

questions.question: Design a service that lets a user reserve an appointment slot for a short period before confirming it.
questions.answer: I would represent a slot with availability and a reservation record carrying owner, expiry and state. Reserving must atomically claim only an available or expired slot, using a conditional update or transaction so two users cannot both win. Confirmation checks ownership and expiry, then transitions the reservation to booked; release or timeout returns capacity safely. A background expiry worker is an optimization, not the correctness mechanism, because delayed jobs must not keep an expired reservation valid. Requests need idempotency so a retry returns the same reservation. I would clarify whether time zones, provider cancellations and rescheduling are in scope.

followups.q: Can a scheduled cleanup alone enforce expiry?
followups.a: No. Every confirmation must check expiry at the authoritative write boundary.

followups.q: What happens if confirmation races expiry?
followups.a: Serialize or condition the transition so exactly one legal state change wins.

questions.trap: Reading availability and then writing a reservation without an atomic claim.

questions.question: How would you model reserving stock for a cart while preventing overselling and handling abandoned carts?
questions.answer: I would distinguish on-hand quantity, reserved quantity and available quantity, with an invariant that reservations never exceed sellable stock. A reservation operation atomically increments reserved units only when enough remain and records a unique cart or order reference. Confirmation converts reserved units to committed inventory; cancellation or expiry releases them exactly once. A reservation state transition and stock adjustment should share a transaction or a durable reconciliation design. Expiry workers may run repeatedly, so release must be idempotent. I would clarify whether stock is global or warehouse-specific and how backorders or late payment confirmation behave.

followups.q: Should cart browsing reserve stock indefinitely?
followups.a: Usually no; use bounded holds or reserve closer to checkout, based on business requirements.

followups.q: How can a duplicate cancellation avoid double release?
followups.a: Condition the reservation state transition and adjust inventory only for the winning transition.

questions.trap: Treating a cached availability read as a guarantee that stock remains available at checkout.

questions.question: Design an import component that validates a CSV file, reports row errors and avoids reprocessing the same upload twice.
questions.answer: I would assign each upload a stable import ID and compute or receive a content fingerprint under a tenant scope to detect retries. The pipeline separates bounded parsing, normalization, row validation and persistence, with row number and stable error codes in the report. Valid rows can be committed in chunks only if the product accepts partial success; otherwise stage them and publish changes after whole-file validation. Limits on file size, row count and field length prevent resource exhaustion. A persisted checkpoint records completed chunks, and the same import ID returns its existing status rather than applying rows again.

followups.q: When should partial success be allowed?
followups.a: Only when the API contract defines which rows commit and how clients correct and resubmit failures.

followups.q: Why stage validated rows?
followups.a: It lets an all-or-nothing import avoid exposing partially applied data before full validation completes.

questions.trap: Loading an unbounded file into memory and assuming a retry cannot duplicate already committed rows.

questions.question: How would you model recurring jobs so two application instances do not run the same occurrence concurrently?
questions.answer: I would distinguish a schedule definition from each durable occurrence. The occurrence has a scheduled time, state, attempt count and ownership lease; workers claim it atomically with a lease expiry so another instance can recover after a crash. A stable occurrence key prevents duplicate creation when the scheduler scans the same interval again. The job handler must tolerate retries because a worker may finish an external effect and die before recording completion. Schedule changes need defined behavior for already materialized occurrences, missed runs and daylight-saving transitions. Metrics should reveal late jobs and repeated failures.

followups.q: Does a lease stop an expired worker from writing?
followups.a: Not by itself; use a fencing token or conditional ownership check on subsequent writes.

followups.q: How do you handle daylight-saving gaps?
followups.a: Define local-time schedule semantics and test ambiguous or nonexistent wall-clock times explicitly.

questions.trap: Assuming a lease alone prevents stale workers from completing after ownership has moved.
questions.notes: Unverified practical LLD estimate. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 7.9 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)).

questions.question: Design an audit record for changes to a user's access role that supports investigation without storing credentials.
questions.answer: I would record the actor or service identity, target identifier, tenant, action, timestamp, correlation ID and a constrained before/after summary that excludes secrets and unnecessary personal data. Audit entries should be append-only for application workflows, with access controls and retention rules separate from ordinary business tables. The role change and audit intent should commit together, often through the same transaction or outbox. A failed audit write must not silently accompany a successful privileged change; the policy should fail closed or use a durable transactional mechanism. I would define who can query records and how tampering or deletion is detected.

followups.q: Should the audit log store the full request body?
followups.a: No. Store only the fields needed for accountability and investigation, with sensitive values excluded.

followups.q: Can ordinary application users edit audit rows?
followups.a: They should not have update/delete privileges; stronger integrity controls depend on the threat model.

questions.trap: Logging complete payloads for convenience, including passwords, bearer tokens or excess personal data.

questions.question: Design a feature-flag evaluator that supports a default, tenant overrides and gradual rollout by user ID.
questions.answer: I would define evaluation precedence explicitly: emergency kill switch, targeted override, rollout rule, then default. Gradual rollout should hash a stable subject identifier with the flag key and a versioned salt, producing deterministic assignment without storing per-request random choices. The evaluator receives an immutable snapshot so one decision does not mix configuration versions. Missing or malformed context should use a documented safe default, especially for security-sensitive flags. Evaluation telemetry should record flag and rule identifiers but avoid sensitive subject data. Configuration validation and audit are separate from the fast read path.

followups.q: Why hash user ID instead of randomizing each request?
followups.a: Stable assignment prevents a user from switching behavior between requests and makes rollout measurable.

followups.q: Should flags decide authorization?
followups.a: A feature flag is not an authorization boundary; access control must remain independently enforced.

questions.trap: Using request randomness for rollout or relying on a feature flag as the only security check.

questions.question: Design an export service that supports CSV and JSON without putting format conditionals throughout business logic.
questions.answer: I would define a format-neutral row or report model, then select a serializer through an explicit format registry at the boundary. Each serializer owns escaping, encoding and output framing, while the query or business policy remains independent of CSV and JSON details. For large exports, stream rows with bounded buffers and propagate cancellation; do not materialize the full report by default. The response should set safe content type and filename rules, and failures after streaming starts need clear client semantics. Contract tests should include commas, quotes, Unicode and empty datasets for each supported format.

followups.q: Should each serializer query the database itself?
followups.a: Prefer separating data retrieval from formatting unless a format-specific query is justified and documented.

followups.q: How do you prevent CSV formula injection?
followups.a: Apply a documented neutralization policy to untrusted cells before emitting spreadsheet-readable files.

questions.trap: Building one giant string with format-specific conditionals in the domain service.

questions.question: How would you apply multiple promotions while preventing incompatible discounts from stacking unexpectedly?
questions.answer: I would represent each promotion with eligibility, effect, priority and an explicit stacking group, then evaluate against an immutable cart snapshot. The policy must say whether discounts combine, compete for the best result or stop after one category; incidental iteration order cannot decide customer price. Money arithmetic needs currency-aware precision and a documented rounding point. The final quote should preserve applied promotion IDs and amounts so checkout can validate the same decision or recompute when cart contents change. Promotions may expire between quote and purchase, so the contract must define whether a quote reserves eligibility or is advisory.

followups.q: Should rules mutate the cart while being evaluated?
followups.a: No. Evaluate against a stable snapshot and produce a result, avoiding order-dependent intermediate state.

followups.q: What if a promotion expires after display?
followups.a: Define a quote validity window or clearly recompute and communicate the changed total at checkout.

questions.trap: Applying discounts in collection order and allowing accidental stacking or repeated application.

questions.question: Design the domain lifecycle for password-reset tokens so replay and account enumeration are controlled.
questions.answer: I would generate a high-entropy, single-use token, store only a verifier or hash, and bind it to an account, purpose and expiry. Redemption atomically marks the token consumed while changing the password, so concurrent replays cannot both succeed. Issuance should avoid revealing whether an address has an account and should rate-limit abuse. A successful reset can revoke existing sessions or refresh tokens according to policy and notify the account owner without including the secret in logs. Expiry cleanup is useful for storage, but redemption must check expiry itself. Responses should not distinguish invalid, expired and unknown-account cases where that leaks identity.

followups.q: Why store a hash rather than the raw reset token?
followups.a: A database read should not directly reveal a usable bearer credential.

followups.q: Is deleting expired tokens enough?
followups.a: No. Every redemption must enforce expiry and consumed state at the time of use.

questions.trap: Logging reset links or accepting a token based only on a prior non-atomic validity read.

questions.question: Design a comment workflow that supports author edits, moderator decisions and an appeal without losing history.
questions.answer: I would separate the current visible comment state from its revision and moderation history. Each edit creates a version with author and timestamp, while moderation records a decision, moderator, reason code and version reviewed. A decision against an old version must not silently hide a newer edit, so commands include the expected version and reject stale actions. Appeal is a new workflow state linked to the prior decision, not destructive replacement. Access rules determine which versions are visible to authors, moderators and readers. Retention and personal-data deletion requirements should be clarified before making the history permanently immutable.

followups.q: Can a moderator decision target the latest comment implicitly?
followups.a: Include the reviewed version so a concurrent edit cannot make the decision ambiguous.

followups.q: Should every edit be public?
followups.a: No. Visibility depends on policy; retain controlled audit history separately from the reader-facing view.

questions.trap: Overwriting a comment in place and losing what moderators actually reviewed.

questions.question: Design a reusable idempotency component for APIs that must replay a prior successful response safely.
questions.answer: I would key records by authenticated caller, operation and client token, and store a request fingerprint plus processing state and response reference. An atomic insert claims a new key; matching completed requests replay the saved outcome, while a different fingerprint conflicts. Concurrent duplicates need a defined in-progress response or bounded wait. The business mutation and completion record should share a transaction when possible; remote effects require their own durable workflow. Retention and cleanup must not erase keys while clients can legitimately retry. The component should not cache sensitive response bodies indiscriminately; store a safe resource reference or minimal replay representation.

followups.q: What status should a duplicate in-flight request receive?
followups.a: A documented conflict or accepted-in-progress response, or a bounded wait; never start the effect twice.

followups.q: Can the component make a remote provider exactly once?
followups.a: No. It protects this API boundary; provider calls need their own idempotency and reconciliation.

questions.trap: Keying only by raw token or storing an unbounded sensitive response forever.

questions.question: How would you model a retry policy so callers cannot accidentally configure an unbounded or unsafe retry loop?
questions.answer: I would make the policy immutable and validate a finite attempt limit, maximum elapsed time, backoff bounds and jitter settings when constructed. It should also define which failure categories are retryable and require the operation owner to state whether repetition is safe or idempotent. Execution receives a deadline and cancellation signal, so a retry cannot outlive the caller's budget. Randomness and time can be injected for deterministic tests. The policy describes decisions, while a separate executor performs waiting and records outcomes. Configuration should reject invalid combinations rather than silently clamp them to surprising values.

followups.q: Should every timeout be retried?
followups.a: No. A timeout may leave the outcome uncertain, and a non-idempotent operation can be duplicated.

followups.q: Why cap elapsed time as well as attempts?
followups.a: Long backoff intervals can exceed a useful request budget even with a modest attempt count.

questions.trap: Treating every exception as retryable and allowing retries with no total deadline.

questions.question: Model a small account-transfer operation so a successful transfer cannot update only one account balance.
questions.answer: I would model a transfer command with source, destination, exact monetary amount, currency and idempotency key, then persist balanced debit and credit entries in one transaction. A ledger entry is append-only; a derived balance may be cached but should reconcile to the authoritative entries. The operation validates distinct accounts and currency compatibility, obtains concurrency protection in a consistent lock order, and records the transfer state and audit reference. A retry with the same key returns the existing result. If accounts live in different services, this atomic design no longer applies and requires a durable multi-step workflow with explicit pending states.

followups.q: Should balance be the only stored truth?
followups.a: For auditable financial movement, preserve entries and treat a balance as a derived or reconciled view.

followups.q: Can one local transaction span independent services?
followups.a: No. Use a durable workflow and communicate pending or compensating outcomes explicitly.

questions.trap: Updating two balances independently or claiming atomicity across separate service databases.
questions.notes: Unverified hypothetical design estimate; not a claim of Harsh's payment-system implementation.

questions.question: Design a simple approval workflow where new approval steps can be added without letting later steps run early.
questions.answer: I would model a workflow definition as an ordered, versioned set of steps and each request as its own durable execution state. A step can start only after its predecessor reaches an accepted terminal result; recording the expected workflow version prevents a definition edit from changing an in-flight request unexpectedly. Each approval action includes actor, decision, timestamp and an idempotency key. Rejection, delegation, timeout and resubmission need explicit transitions. A registry can supply step handlers, but ordering and authorization remain centrally enforced. Adding a step should require configuration and handler tests without changing unrelated step behavior.

followups.q: Can a workflow edit affect an active request?
followups.a: Define pinning semantics; commonly each execution retains the definition version it started with.

followups.q: How do you prevent duplicate approval submissions?
followups.a: Use an action key and conditional state transition so only one decision is applied.

questions.trap: Storing only a current step number with no definition version, actor audit or transition guard.

questions.question: What are the creational, structural and behavioural design patterns, with Spring examples?
questions.answer: Creational patterns control object creation: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder and Prototype. Structural patterns compose objects: Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade, Composite, Bridge and Flyweight. Behavioural patterns govern interaction: Strategy, Observer, Template Method, Command, Chain of Responsibility, State, Iterator, Mediator and Visitor. Spring shows many of them. Singleton is the default bean scope; BeanFactory and FactoryBean are factories; AOP proxies back @Transactional and @Async; JdbcTemplate and RestTemplate use Template Method; ApplicationEvent implements Observer; UriComponentsBuilder is a builder; HandlerAdapter is an adapter.

followups.q: Which pattern does @Transactional rely on?
followups.a: Proxy: an AOP proxy intercepts the call to add transaction behaviour.

followups.q: Where does Spring use Template Method?
followups.a: JdbcTemplate and RestTemplate fix the workflow and let you supply the varying part.

questions.trap: Listing pattern names without one real example for each family.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 7.6 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S12-038, JH-S06-005.

questions.question: What is the Prototype pattern, and how do Builder and Factory differ?
questions.answer: Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing one instead of constructing it from scratch, which helps when construction is expensive. In Java prefer a copy constructor over Cloneable, and watch shallow versus deep copies; Spring's prototype scope, a new bean per request, is related in spirit. Builder solves complex objects with many optional parameters, building one type step by step and avoiding telescoping constructors, for example Employee.builder().name("A").build(). Factory decides which implementation of a common interface to create from a key, for example NotifierFactory.get("SMS"). They combine well: a factory can return a builder, and a builder that validates in build() makes immutable objects easy.

followups.q: Why is Object.clone discouraged?
followups.a: It is shallow by default, depends on Cloneable's odd contract and is easy to get wrong; copy constructors are clearer.

followups.q: When would you pick Builder over Factory?
followups.a: When one type has many optional fields; use Factory when the question is which type to create.

questions.trap: Treating Builder and Factory as the same pattern. One shapes construction, the other chooses the type.
